title: Asteroids and Comets
slideFile: none (no teacher slides; Cosmic Perspective 10th ed. Ch 12.1-12.3)
intro: Trillions of leftovers from the birth of the planets still orbit the Sun. Learn how asteroids, comets and dwarf planets differ (and why Pluto was reclassified), what separates a meteor from a meteorite, and what asteroids are like up close, from rubble piles to layered Vesta and icy Ceres. Read the story of the early solar system in meteorites, find out why Jupiter kept a planet from forming in the asteroid belt and carved the Kirkwood gaps, then follow a comet sunward to see why its tails always point away from the Sun, where meteor showers come from, and how the Kuiper belt and Oort cloud got their comets.

learningObjectives.text: What's the difference between an asteroid, a comet, and a dwarf planet?
What do meteorites tell us about asteroids?
Why is there an asteroid belt?

sections.title: Leftovers from the birth of the planets

img.alt: Three panels. Asteroid: a lumpy grey-brown rock, a rocky leftover planetesimal, mostly between Mars and Jupiter. Comet: a lumpy icy body speckled with dust, an icy leftover that mostly stays frozen far beyond Neptune. Dwarf planet: a round body, big enough to be round; it can be a large asteroid such as Ceres or a large comet such as Pluto or Eris.

steps.title: Strength in numbers
bullets: Besides the planets, the Sun is orbited by enormous numbers of **small bodies**, from specks of dust up to **Pluto** and **Eris**. There are probably **trillions** of them.
All of them are **leftovers from planet formation**: they formed early in the solar system's history but never became part of a full-size planet.
Our picture of these objects has been transformed over the past few decades, which has also made them harder to define and classify.

img.alt: Three cards. Time capsules: many small bodies have barely changed in 4.5 billion years, so they hold clues to how the solar system was born. Delivery service: they probably brought Earth water and other ingredients for life. Impacts: they left craters on Earth and sometimes changed the course of evolution.

steps.title: Why small bodies matter
bullets: Many have barely changed since they formed about **4½ billion years ago**, so their makeup, locations and numbers hold clues to how the solar system was born, a bit like studying how furniture is made from the scraps on a carpenter's floor.
Asteroids or comets probably **delivered water** and other ingredients that helped make life on Earth possible.
Their occasional **impacts** have scarred Earth with craters and sometimes changed the course of evolution. Comet sightings have even changed history when people acted on superstitions about them.

img.alt: Flowchart: does it orbit the Sun and is it too small to be a planet? Then what is it made of? Rock and metal means asteroid; ice and rocky dust means comet. Either one that is big enough for gravity to pull it round is also a dwarf planet: Ceres is a rocky one; Pluto, Eris, Makemake and Haumea are icy ones.

steps.title: Today's simple definitions
bullets: Both asteroids and comets **orbit the Sun** and are **too small to be planets**.
An **asteroid** is a **rocky** leftover planetesimal; a **comet** is an **ice-rich** one.
A **dwarf planet** is a small body, asteroid or comet, that is **large enough to be round**. The category has only been used since **2006**.

boxes.text: Small bodies never became part of a planet, so many of them still preserve the raw ingredients and conditions of the solar system's earliest days.
Rocky = asteroid, icy = comet, round = dwarf planet (which can be either).

A dwarf planet is not a third material: it is an asteroid or a comet that happens to be big enough to be round (Book 12.1, p. 353). The dwarf planet category dates from 2006, not from Pluto's discovery in 1930.

sections.title: Asteroids: starlike points of light

img.alt: Animation on a black star field: the stars stay as sharp dots while a small asteroid drifts across, leaving a short streak, as in a long-exposure photo. Asteroids are found by this motion against the stars.

steps.title: Why 'starlike'?
bullets: The word **asteroid** means **'starlike'**, but nothing about asteroids is starlike. The name dates from when all we knew was that they looked like **points of light** in telescopes, because they are so small.
Asteroids are usually picked out in telescope images by their **motion relative to the stars**. In a long-exposure photo the stars are dots and an asteroid makes a **short streak**.

img.alt: Timeline: 1801, Ceres found and called a planet, about 20 years after Uranus; 1802, William Herschel offers the word asteroid, meaning starlike; over the next 7 years Pallas, Juno and Vesta are found and called minor planets; later, discoveries speed up and asteroid becomes the usual word. Today hundreds of thousands are catalogued.

steps.title: From planet to minor planet
bullets: The first asteroid, **Ceres**, was found in **1801**, only about 20 years after Uranus. It was first called a **planet**, and later proved to be the largest asteroid.
**Pallas, Juno and Vesta** followed over the next 7 years. Once astronomers realized how small these objects were, they called them **'minor planets'**.

**William Herschel**, who discovered Uranus with his sister **Caroline**, had suggested the word 'asteroid' in **1802**, but it only caught on decades later, once discoveries came fast and it was clear most of them lie **between Mars and Jupiter**.

img.alt: Three steps: 1, spotted and given a provisional name from the year, month and order of discovery, for example 2027 AA for the first found in January 2027; 2, tracked until its orbit is worked out with the law of gravity; 3, named by the discoverer with approval from the International Astronomical Union.

steps.title: How asteroids get names
bullets: **Hundreds of thousands** have been catalogued, and more are found almost every night.
A new asteroid first gets a **provisional name** from its discovery year, month and order: the first found in January 2027 would be **2027 AA** (numbers are added when the letters run out).

Once its orbit has been calculated with the law of gravity, the discoverer may name it, with approval from the **International Astronomical Union**. The earliest carry names from **mythology**; newer ones honour scientists, authors, celebrities, cartoon heroes and even pets.

boxes.text: An asteroid's light is just reflected sunlight from a tiny body, so even a big telescope shows only a point. Its motion is what gives it away.
Aster = star (as in asterisk): 'asteroid' = 'star-like', named for its looks, not its nature.

Ceres was called a planet in 1801, then a minor planet; today it is both the largest asteroid and a dwarf planet (Book 12.1, pp. 351-353). The word 'asteroid' was coined in 1802 but did not come into wide use until many decades later.

sections.title: Comets in our sky

img.alt: Night sky with stars and the same comet drawn four times, on nights 1, 4, 7 and 10, each a little farther along with its tail. Over minutes or hours it stays with the stars; its drift shows only over many days, and it can hang in the sky for weeks.

steps.title: Fuzzy balls with long tails
bullets: For most of history comets were known only from the sky. Every few years one becomes visible to the **naked eye** as a **fuzzy ball with a long tail**. The word comet comes from the Greek for **'hair'**.
Comets sometimes changed history: the ancient Chinese believed a comet announced a time of major upheaval, so sightings often triggered such change.

Photos can make a comet look as if it races across the sky, but it does **not**. Over minutes or hours it stays nearly fixed among the stars (rising and setting with them); its drift against the constellations shows only over **many days**, and it may stay visible for **weeks**.

img.alt: Timeline: 1577, Tycho Brahe shows a comet is far beyond the Moon; late 1600s, Newton shows comets orbit the Sun; 1705, Halley calculates that the 1682 comet returns every 76 years; 1758, it returns as predicted and is named for him; 1986, last pass; 2061, next return.

steps.title: From omen to orbit
bullets: Comets were usually thought to be inside Earth's atmosphere until **1577**, when **Tycho Brahe** compared observations from different places in Europe and proved a comet was **far beyond the Moon**.
About a century later **Newton** worked out that comets **orbit the Sun**.

In **1705** **Edmond Halley** used Newton's law of gravitation to show that the comet of 1682 had been seen many times before and orbits the Sun every **76 years**. He predicted its return in **1758**; it came back on time, after his death, and was named for him. It last passed through the inner solar system in **1986** and returns in **2061**.

img.alt: Side-by-side comparison. Asteroid: rock and metal, formed mostly inside the frost line, mostly in the belt at 2-3 AU, no tail. Comet: ice with rocky dust, formed in the cold outer solar system, mostly in the Kuiper belt or Oort cloud, grows a coma and tails only near the Sun.

steps.title: Most comets never grow tails
bullets: The **vast majority** of comets have **no tails** and never come close to Earth. They stay frozen far beyond Neptune, in the **Kuiper belt** and the **Oort cloud**.
The comets we see are rare ones whose orbits were changed by the gravity of planets, other comets or passing stars, sending them into the inner solar system.
Most will not return for thousands of years, if ever. A few, like Halley's, are pushed onto elliptical orbits that bring them back **periodically**.

img.alt: The name Comet 67P/Churyumov-Gerasimenko split into parts: 67P means the 67th known periodic comet, one that keeps returning; Churyumov-Gerasimenko are its two discoverers. A note says the SOHO spacecraft had found more than 4000 Sun-grazing comets by 2022.

steps.title: Naming comets
bullets: Comets are named for the first observers (up to **three**) to report them to the International Astronomical Union, plus other labels.
**Comet 67P/Churyumov-Gerasimenko**: '67P' means the 67th known **periodic** comet (one that returns again and again); the rest is its two discoverers.
The champion comet finder is the **SOHO** solar observatory spacecraft: more than **4000 'Sun-grazing'** comets by 2022, most of them on their **last** pass by the Sun.

boxes.text: A comet is far away compared with anything in our atmosphere, so its motion across the sky is slow. What moves it from night to night is its orbit around the Sun.
Halley: 76 years, last 1986, next 2061 (1986 + 76 = 2062, so 'about' 76).

Comets do NOT streak across the sky like meteors; a comet hangs among the stars for weeks (Book 12.1, p. 351). Most comets have no tail at all. Halley discovered the comet's period, not the comet itself, which had been seen many times before.

sections.title: Pluto, Eris and the dwarf planets

img.alt: Nearly edge-on view of the Sun with the flat orbits of the planets out to Neptune, and Pluto's orbit drawn as a longer, tilted ellipse crossing them. Caption: Pluto is tiny, about 0.2% of Earth's mass, ice-rich, on a stretched and tilted orbit in the middle of the Kuiper belt.

steps.title: Pluto, the misfit planet
bullets: **Pluto** was called a planet after its discovery in **1930**, but it never fit: it is tiny (about **0.2% of Earth's mass**), **ice-rich**, and its orbit is far more **elliptical** and more **tilted** to the ecliptic than any planet's.

By the **1950s** astronomers realized that many comets visiting the inner solar system come from the **Kuiper belt** region, and Pluto orbits near the **middle** of it. Pluto began to look like an unusually large **comet**.
In the **1990s** other Pluto-like objects were found there, just smaller. Pluto was not so unusual after all.

img.alt: Pluto and Eris drawn side by side at about the same size. Eris, found in 2005, is about 27% more massive than Pluto and has a moon, Dysnomia. Question below: if Pluto is a planet, must Eris be one too, and what about slightly smaller bodies?

steps.title: Eris forces the question
bullets: Larger and larger Kuiper belt objects turned up, and in **2005** Caltech astronomer **Michael Brown** announced **Eris**: about Pluto's size but about **27% more massive**, with a moon named **Dysnomia**.
Eris is named after a Greek goddess of strife (a nod to the arguments it caused); Dysnomia was her daughter, a goddess of lawlessness.
If Pluto was a planet, then surely the more massive Eris was too. But what about objects only slightly smaller? Or, since they all have comet-like makeup, should they all be called comets?

img.alt: List of the five official dwarf planets with small globes: Pluto, Kuiper belt, found 1930; Eris, Kuiper belt, found 2005, 27% more massive than Pluto; Makemake, Kuiper belt; Haumea, Kuiper belt, oblong from fast spin; Ceres, asteroid belt, found 1801. Dozens more may join.

steps.title: The dwarf planet category (2006)
bullets: In **2006** the **International Astronomical Union** created the **dwarf planet** category for small bodies large enough to be **round**.
Official dwarf planets: **Pluto, Eris, Makemake and Haumea** in the Kuiper belt, and the asteroid **Ceres**. (Haumea is oblong, but only because it spins fast; it would otherwise be round.)

Because the definition depends on roundness, and distant shapes are hard to know, **dozens more** may join the list. There may also be undiscovered dwarf planets, or even larger objects such as a hypothesized 'Planet 9', that could reopen the definition of planet.

img.alt: Two overlapping circles, rocky and icy. Most asteroids sit on the rocky side and small comets on the icy side. Ceres sits in the overlap, rocky but with surface ice that can vaporize. Kuiper belt objects of every size, all ice and rock, sit on the icy side; they are also called KBOs or TNOs.

steps.title: Fuzzy boundaries
bullets: In practice: asteroids are **rocky** leftover planetesimals, comets **icy** ones, and dwarf planets are either kind, if round. Yet there can be debate over whether something is 'round enough'.
Compositions also **overlap**: some asteroids, including **Ceres**, seem to have enough ice near their surface to lose some to vaporization, as comets do.

In the **Kuiper belt** everything, from boulders to dwarf planets, is probably ice and rock: essentially comets of different sizes, the **comets of the Kuiper belt**. Since some astronomers object to calling tail-less bodies comets, they are also called **Kuiper belt objects (KBOs)** or **trans-Neptunian objects (TNOs)**.

boxes.text: Nature makes a smooth range of sizes and mixtures of rock and ice. Any human category has to draw a line somewhere through that range, which is why the edges stay fuzzy.
Five official dwarfs: 'Please Eat More Healthy Cereal' = Pluto, Eris, Makemake, Haumea, Ceres.

Eris is about the same SIZE as Pluto but about 27% more MASSIVE (Book 12.1, p. 353). Ceres is the only dwarf planet in the asteroid belt; Vesta is NOT an official dwarf planet (as of 2022). Haumea counts even though it is oblong, because its shape comes from fast spin.

sections.title: Meteors and meteorites

img.alt: Three cards. Meteor, meaning a thing in the air: the flash of light when dust or rock hits the air at high speed. Fireball: an unusually bright meteor made by a rock big enough to survive. Meteorite, meaning associated with meteors: the rock found on the ground.

steps.title: A meteor is a flash of light
bullets: People often mix up the words, but a **meteor** ('a thing in the air', like meteorology) is only the **flash of light** made when a particle of dust or rock enters our atmosphere at high speed. It is **not** the particle itself.
Meteors are also called **shooting stars** or **falling stars**, because people once thought they really were stars falling from the sky.

img.alt: Animation of the sky above the ground. A pea-size grain streaks in and burns up completely high in the air: a meteor. A larger rock makes a very bright fireball all the way down and lands as a dark stone: a meteorite.

steps.title: Most burn up; a few land
bullets: The **vast majority** of meteor particles are **no bigger than peas** and **burn up completely** before reaching the ground.
Only rarely is a chunk of rock big enough to survive the plunge and leave a **meteorite** ('associated with meteors') on the ground.
Those rare cases make unusually bright meteors called **fireballs**.

img.alt: Map of the inner solar system: a big arrow brings meteorites from the asteroid belt to Earth; a thin dashed arrow brings a few from Mars, and a few come from the Moon. Almost all meteorites are tiny asteroids or pieces of them; lunar and martian meteorites were blasted off by impacts.

steps.title: Why fireball finds are precious
bullets: Observers find a **few meteorites each year** by following the paths of fireballs.
These finds are especially valuable: their paths can be **traced back** to show where they came from, and they can be collected **before Earth material contaminates** them.

boxes.text: The particle moves so fast that it heats the air around it until the air glows. Small grains vaporize long before they reach the ground.
Meteor = in the air (light). Meteorite = on the ground (rock): 'ite' as in a rock name, like granite.
A meteor is the LIGHT, not the rock; a meteorite is the rock that reached the ground (Book 12.1, p. 354). Most meteors leave no meteorite at all.

sections.title: Rocks that fall from the sky

img.alt: Timeline of belief about falling stones: Anaxagoras in ancient Greece concludes they fall from the heavens; Thomas Jefferson doubts a fall in Connecticut; today more than 1000 falls have been seen and tens of thousands of meteorites catalogued. Notes: falls often break up over several kilometres, only one reliable record of a death (1888), and most land in the ocean.

steps.title: Do stones really fall from the sky?
bullets: Stories of **'fallen stars'** led the ancient Greek philosopher **Anaxagoras** to conclude that meteorites fall from the heavens and that planets and stars are flaming rocks. That made him the first person known to think the heavens and Earth are made of the **same materials**.

Many later scientists were doubtful. Hearing of a meteorite fall in Connecticut, **Thomas Jefferson** reportedly joked that it was easier to believe professors would lie than that stones would fall from heaven.
Today more than **1000 falls** have been seen and **tens of thousands** of meteorites catalogued. Falling meteorites often **break apart**, scattering pieces over several kilometres.
A direct hit would be fatal, yet there is only **one** reliable account of a death (in 1888, near Sulaymaniyah, Iraq). Most meteorites fall into the **ocean**, which covers three-fourths of Earth.

img.alt: Four clue cards: 1, a dark, pitted crust from the fiery fall; 2, metal-rich enough to pull a magnet on a string; 3, rare elements such as iridium; 4, isotope ratios unlike Earth rocks. Lab analysis is the final test.

steps.title: How to tell a meteorite from an Earth rock
bullets: Meteorites usually have a **dark, pitted crust** from their fiery fall through the air.
Some are so **metal-rich** they attract a magnet hanging on a string.

The final test is the **lab**: meteorites often contain elements such as **iridium** that are very rare in Earth rocks, and even common elements come in different **isotope ratios**. Many museums will analyze a small chip for free.

img.alt: Map of the inner solar system: a big arrow brings meteorites from the asteroid belt to Earth; a thin dashed arrow brings a few from Mars, and a few come from the Moon. Almost all meteorites are tiny asteroids or pieces of them; lunar and martian meteorites were blasted off by impacts.

steps.title: Where meteorites come from
bullets: Every meteorite whose fall was observed or filmed came from the **asteroid belt**. So the vast majority of meteorites are **very small asteroids or pieces of asteroids**.
A few match the **Moon** or **Mars**. Moderately large impacts can blast surface rock into space, where it orbits the Sun until it lands on another world.
These **lunar and martian meteorites** are direct samples of the Moon and Mars, which makes them very valuable.

boxes.text: A rock from space has never been mixed into Earth's crust, so its chemistry (iridium, isotope ratios) carries a fingerprint that Earth rocks lack.
Crust, magnet, iridium, isotopes: 'Can Meteorites Imitate Earth? No!'
Most meteorites come from the ASTEROID BELT, not from comets (Book 12.1, p. 355); a few come from the Moon and Mars. A dark crust alone does not prove a meteorite; lab analysis is the final test.

sections.title: Asteroid sizes and shapes

img.alt: Bar chart of how common asteroids are by size: one Ceres, just under 1000 km; about a dozen large ones the size of medium moons; probably more than a million over 1 km; and many more smaller still. Bars show the trend only.

steps.title: A huge range of sizes
bullets: Spacecraft pictures show asteroids in a wide variety of **sizes and shapes**, covered in **craters** from impacts over time. **Hundreds of thousands** more have been studied with telescopes.
**Ceres**, the largest, is **just under 1000 km** across, a little over a quarter of the Moon's diameter. About a **dozen** others would count as medium-size moons if they orbited a planet.
Smaller asteroids are far more common: probably **more than a million** are over **1 km** across, and many more are smaller.

img.alt: Three bodies from small to large: small asteroids are potato-shaped, sometimes two touching or loose rubble piles; large ones such as Pallas and Vesta are not far from round; Ceres, just under 1000 km, is round enough to count as a dwarf planet. Arrow: bigger body, stronger gravity, rounder shape.

steps.title: Gravity sets the shape
bullets: Most asteroids are **not spherical**. Shape depends mainly on the strength of **gravity**.
Only large asteroids have gravity strong enough to mold them into roughly round shapes. Only **Ceres** is round enough to be a dwarf planet, though **Pallas** and **Vesta** are not far off.
Smaller asteroids look like **potatoes**. Some apparent single asteroids are probably **two or more objects** touching, held by weak gravity; others are weakly bound **piles of rubble**.

img.alt: A large dark asteroid and a smaller shiny one look equally bright in visible light. The dark one absorbs more sunlight, so it is warmer and brighter in infrared. Comparing visible and infrared gives reflectivity; with distance from the orbit, the size follows: the darker one must be bigger.

steps.title: Size from brightness
bullets: How can we know sizes when most asteroids look like points? An asteroid's **brightness** depends on its **size, distance and reflectivity**. At the same distance and reflectivity, the brighter one is bigger.
**Distance** comes from where it is in its orbit.

**Reflectivity** comes from comparing **visible** brightness (reflected sunlight) with **infrared** brightness (heat, which shows how much sunlight it absorbs). Then reflectivity and distance give the **size**.

img.alt: Animation: a long potato-shaped asteroid spins while a graph of its brightness is drawn. The brightness rises when the long side faces us and falls when the end faces us, giving two peaks per turn.

steps.title: Shape from a flickering light
bullets: A nonspherical asteroid with an evenly bright surface reflects **more light** when it turns its **larger side** toward the Sun and our telescopes, so its brightness rises and falls as it **rotates**.
For asteroids that pass close to Earth, astronomers have also mapped shapes by bouncing **radar** signals off them.

boxes.text: A small body's gravity is too weak to reshape its rock into a ball, so it stays irregular, like a potato.
Brightness = size x reflectivity, dimmed by distance. Know two, find the third.

Two asteroids equally bright at the same distance are NOT necessarily the same size: the darker (less reflective) one must be larger (Book 12.2, p. 356). Pallas and Vesta are nearly round but are not official dwarf planets; only Ceres is.

sections.title: Mass, density and composition

img.alt: Animation: the tiny moon Dactyl circles the elongated asteroid Ida. Measuring the moon's orbital period and distance, then using Newton's version of Kepler's third law, gives Ida's mass.

steps.title: Weighing an asteroid with its moon
bullets: The most direct way to measure mass is to watch an object's **gravity pull on something else**. That is possible only for asteroids visited by spacecraft or with small **moons** of their own.
The asteroid **Ida** has a tiny moon, **Dactyl**. Dactyl's **orbital period** and **distance** plug into **Newton's version of Kepler's third law** to give Ida's mass.
Precise masses are known for only **a few dozen** asteroids, but they let us estimate others.

img.alt: Bar chart of density: Eros 2.4 grams per cubic centimetre, close to solid rock; Mathilde 1.5, a loose rubble pile; water 1.0 for comparison; Halley's comet nucleus below 1, ice plus empty space.

steps.title: Density: solid rock or rubble pile?
bullets: **Density = mass / volume** (the volume comes from size measurements). Density reveals an asteroid's origin and makeup.
**Eros** and **Mathilde** look alike in pictures, but Eros has a density of **2.4 g/cm³**, about what solid rock of its size should have.
Mathilde's **1.5 g/cm³** is so low that it must be a loosely bound **rubble pile** held together by weak gravity, not a solid chunk.

img.alt: Strip across the asteroid belt from about 2 to 3.5 AU. Inner part: stony asteroids of rock and metal, formed inside the frost line. Beyond about 2.5 AU carbon compounds condense; beyond about 2.7 AU, where the frost line may have been, asteroids are dark, carbon-rich and hold some water, as Ceres does. A few asteroids are mostly metal: pieces of shattered cores.

steps.title: Composition from spectra
bullets: Spectral lines are 'fingerprints' of chemical makeup. Thousands of asteroid spectra agree with the theory of solar system formation.
Asteroids are mostly **metal and rock**, because they condensed **inside the frost line**.

Those toward the **outer** edge of the belt hold more **dark, carbon-rich** material, which could condense only in the cooler outer region; some even hold a little **water**, so they formed near the frost line.
A few are mostly **metal**, such as iron: probably fragments of the **metal cores of shattered worlds**.

boxes.text: Mass alone cannot tell a solid rock from a loose pile; dividing by volume can. Empty spaces between the rubble make the average density low.
Solid rock about 2.4 (Eros), rubble pile about 1.5 (Mathilde), comet nucleus under 1 (Halley), in g/cm³.

A low density does not have to mean ice: Mathilde's 1.5 g/cm³ is explained by gaps in a rubble pile (Book 12.2, p. 356). Mass needs a second object to pull on (a moon or a spacecraft); brightness gives size, not mass.

sections.title: Asteroids up close

img.alt: Cut-away of Vesta: a flattened ball, nearly 25% wider than tall, with a metal core, a rocky mantle and a crust, and a huge south-pole crater with a 23 km high central peak. Notes: rock at the crater floor matches deep interior rock and many meteorites; signs of volcanic rock but no volcanoes seen; ridges ring the equator.

steps.title: Dawn at Vesta
bullets: The **Dawn** mission orbited **Vesta** for about 14 months in **2011-12**, then studied **Ceres** from orbit from **2015 to 2018**. It will stay in orbit around Ceres, a tiny dead moon.

Vesta is nearly **25% wider** at the equator than it is tall, probably because a huge impact gouged out a giant **crater at its south pole**. Vesta was likely once much rounder, which raises the question of whether it should be a dwarf planet (no decision as of 2022).
The crater's **central mountain** (a rebound peak) rises **23 km**, one of the tallest mountains in the solar system.

img.alt: Animation: a rocky asteroid heats up and melts inside; metal dots sink to the centre and rock rises, making a core, mantle and crust. Then a collision shatters it. Core pieces become metal-rich processed meteorites; mantle and crust pieces become rocky processed meteorites.

steps.title: Vesta's layers and its lost pieces
bullets: The impact dug so deep that rock at the crater floor matches what we expect **deep inside terrestrial worlds**. This confirms Vesta is big enough to have **differentiated**: a **metal core**, a low-density rocky **crust** and a **mantle** between.
The crater-floor rock's spectrum matches **many small asteroids and meteorites**, which are probably **pieces of Vesta** blasted off by that impact.

Mysteries remain: parts of the surface look like **volcanic rock**, yet no volcanoes or lava flows have been seen (perhaps hidden by billions of years of craters), and unexplained **ridges** ring its equator.

img.alt: Ceres drawn as a cratered grey ball with bright salty spots in one crater and a lone 4 km mountain. Notes: nearly as massive as the rest of the asteroid belt combined; lots of water ice; bright spots are salts left by groundwater; more ammonia compounds than expected.

steps.title: Ceres: the largest asteroid
bullets: **Ceres** holds nearly as much **mass** as the rest of the asteroid belt combined. Its **low density** and outer-belt location suggested lots of **water ice**, and Dawn confirmed it.

**Bright spots** in some craters are **salts** and other reflective minerals, probably brought up by **groundwater** and left behind when the water vaporized into space. The crater with the brightest spots sometimes fills with **haze**.

A single tall **4 km mountain** stands alone; no one knows how it formed. Otherwise Ceres has craters and tectonic cracks, as expected, but more **ammonia** compounds than expected for a body formed inside the frost line.

img.alt: Four rows: Itokawa, Hayabusa from Japan, 500 m long, sample returned 2010; Ryugu, Hayabusa2, sample returned 2020; Bennu, NASA's OSIRIS-REx, carbon-rich, sampled 2020 and due home 2023; next, OSIRIS-APEX to Apophis, plus the Lucy, DART and Psyche missions.

steps.title: Bringing samples home
bullets: Spacecraft have visited more than a dozen smaller asteroids, and three missions collected **samples**: Japan's **Hayabusa** returned dust from **Itokawa** (500 m long) in 2010; **Hayabusa2** returned samples of **Ryugu** in 2020; NASA's **OSIRIS-REx** scooped up **Bennu** in 2020, due back in 2023.

All three look like **rubble piles**. Bennu is a **carbon-rich** asteroid that may resemble the objects that brought Earth ingredients for oceans, air and life. Its surface was so loose that the spacecraft might have sunk in.
Next: **OSIRIS-APEX** goes on to **Apophis**, whose orbit passes near Earth; plus the **Lucy**, **DART** and **Psyche** missions.

boxes.text: A big impact works like a drill: it digs through a world's outer layers and exposes, and throws out, rock from deep inside.
Dawn: Vesta first (2011-12), then Ceres (2015-18). V before C, as in the alphabet backward.

Vesta's lopsided shape comes from an impact crater, not from fast spin (that is Haumea) (Book 12.2, p. 356). Ceres's bright spots are salts, not exposed ice. The samples came from Itokawa, Ryugu and Bennu, not from Vesta or Ceres.

sections.title: Two kinds of meteorite

img.alt: Tree diagram: meteorites split into primitive (chondrites, unchanged, 4.56 billion years old) and processed (achondrites, from a larger body that melted, slightly younger). Primitive: stony, rock with metal flakes; carbon-rich, with carbon compounds and sometimes water. Processed: metal-rich, iron and nickel like a core; rocky, like mantle or crust rock, some like basalt.

steps.title: Primitive and processed
bullets: Tens of thousands of meteorites are free asteroid samples. Thousands analyzed in detail fall into two basic types.

**Primitive** meteorites are remnants from the birth of the solar system, essentially **unchanged** since they first clumped together in the solar nebula. Radiometric dating shows they are the **oldest rocks** in the solar system. They are also called **chondrites**, after the roundish grains (**chondrules**) in them.

**Processed** meteorites were once part of a **larger object** that 'processed' the original nebula material into another form. They are slightly **younger** than primitive ones and lack chondrules, so they are called **achondrites**.

img.alt: Simplified drawings of four sliced meteorites: stony primitive, rock dotted with shiny metal flakes; carbon-rich primitive, dark with small whitish round grains; metal-rich processed, solid metal; rocky processed, like volcanic rock, some from Vesta.

steps.title: Four subtypes
bullets: **Stony primitive**: rocky minerals with a small but noticeable share of shiny **metal flakes**.
**Carbon-rich primitive**: also rocky, but with lots of **carbon compounds** and sometimes a little **water** bound in the rock.
**Metal-rich processed**: mostly dense **iron and nickel** with small amounts of other metals, like the **cores** of terrestrial planets.
**Rocky processed**: lower density, made of rock like terrestrial **mantles and crusts**; a few are remarkably close to the **basalts** erupted by volcanoes.

boxes.text: Primitive means 'first', not 'crude': these rocks have never been melted, so they still record conditions at the start of the solar system.
Chondrite = has chondrules = primitive. A-chondrite = 'without' chondrules = processed.
Processed meteorites are slightly YOUNGER than primitive ones, not older (Book 12.2, p. 358). Metal-rich meteorites are processed, not primitive, even though primitive ones contain metal flakes.

steps.title: The solar system's starting date
bullets: Precise radiometric dating gives primitive meteorites an age of **4.56 billion years**, so that is when **accretion** in the solar nebula began.

Their **metal flakes** may be the tiny particles that first **condensed** from the nebula's gas. Their small roundish grains may be **solidified droplets** splashed out of small planetesimals as they grew.
The **vast majority** of meteorites are primitive, so even 4½ billion years later, huge numbers of small leftovers from planet formation still orbit the Sun.

Beyond 2.5 AU carbon compounds could condense, and the frost line may have been as close as 2.7 AU: carbon-rich primitive meteorites, some with water, from the outer belt.

steps.title: Stony or carbon-rich? It depends on distance
bullets: By the nebular theory most meteorites formed **inside the frost line**, so they are metal and rock.

Models say that beyond about **2.5 AU** from the Sun the nebula was cool enough for **carbon compounds** to condense. So **carbon-rich** primitive meteorites come from **beyond** that distance and **stony** ones from **closer in**.
Lab studies agree: carbon-rich meteorites match the dark, carbon-rich asteroids of the **outer** belt; stony meteorites match asteroids of the **inner** belt.

steps.title: Water and the frost line
bullets: Meteorites and computer models suggest the **frost line** may have been as close as **2.7 AU**, just beyond where carbon compounds condensed.
Asteroids that formed beyond it, such as **Ceres**, hold a small but significant fraction of **water**.
That may be enough to make them the bodies that brought the terrestrial planets **water, carbon-rich compounds** and other ingredients for habitability and life.

boxes.text: What could condense from the nebula depended on temperature, and temperature depended on distance from the young Sun. So a meteorite's chemistry is a record of its birthplace.
2.5 AU: carbon; 2.7 AU: water (C comes before W, closer in).
4.56 billion years is the age of the oldest solids, i.e. when accretion BEGAN, not when Earth finished forming (Book 12.2, p. 358). Carbon-rich meteorites formed FARTHER from the Sun than stony ones.

sections.title: What processed meteorites tell us

img.alt: Animation: a rocky asteroid heats up and melts inside; metal dots sink to the centre and rock rises, making a core, mantle and crust. Then a collision shatters it. Core pieces become metal-rich processed meteorites; mantle and crust pieces become rocky processed meteorites.

steps.title: Pieces of worlds that melted
bullets: Processed meteorites look like the **cores, mantles or crusts** of terrestrial worlds. They are fragments of larger asteroids that underwent **differentiation**: their interiors **melted**, so **metals sank** to the centre and **rock rose** to the surface.
That explains why there are two types of processed meteorite.

img.alt: Tree diagram: meteorites split into primitive (chondrites, unchanged, 4.56 billion years old) and processed (achondrites, from a larger body that melted, slightly younger). Primitive: stony, rock with metal flakes; carbon-rich, with carbon compounds and sometimes water. Processed: metal-rich, iron and nickel like a core; rocky, like mantle or crust rock, some like basalt.

steps.title: Metal-rich: a dissected planet
bullets: **Metal-rich** meteorites come from large asteroids that differentiated and were later **shattered** in collisions: pieces of a 'dissected planet'.
They are valuable because we cannot drill down to Earth's core, and they **prove** that large worlds really do differentiate, confirming what seismic studies of Earth suggest.
They also show that **world-shattering collisions** must have been common early in the solar system's history.

img.alt: Cut-away of Vesta: a flattened ball, nearly 25% wider than tall, with a metal core, a rocky mantle and a crust, and a huge south-pole crater with a 23 km high central peak. Notes: rock at the crater floor matches deep interior rock and many meteorites; signs of volcanic rock but no volcanoes seen; ridges ring the equator.

steps.title: Rocky: lava on early asteroids
bullets: **Rocky** processed meteorites come from the **mantles or crusts** of differentiated worlds. Many, including those that seem to come from **Vesta**, are so close to Earth's volcanic rocks that they must have formed in **lava flows**.

So some large asteroids were once **volcanically active**, and pieces of their surfaces were chipped off by smaller asteroids. Besides Vesta, perhaps **a few dozen** others were active soon after the solar system formed.
These meteorites date to only **millions of years** after the solar system's birth, so the active period was **short**: the interiors **cooled quickly**.

img.alt: Three cards from small to large: small asteroids are geologically dead with only craters; bodies a few hundred kilometres and up had enough heat to melt and differentiate; Vesta and a few dozen others were volcanically active early on, but only briefly before cooling.

steps.title: Size decides geology
bullets: Small asteroids are geologically **'dead'**, with **impact craters** as their only features; many are basically primitive meteorites that are still in orbit.
Worlds larger than **a few hundred kilometres** across had enough heat to **melt and differentiate**; some, like Vesta, were volcanic early on.

Dwarf planets like Ceres, and 'almost dwarf planets' like Vesta, are **planetlike** in almost every way. We may care about labels; nature does not. Only **size and composition** matter, and geology follows.

boxes.text: Only worlds larger than a few hundred kilometres held enough heat to melt, separate into layers and erupt lava, and even they cooled within millions of years.
Core = metal-rich meteorite. Mantle or crust = rocky processed meteorite.
Metal-rich meteorites need BOTH steps: differentiation first, then a shattering collision (Book 12.2, p. 359). Small asteroids never melted, so they are not the source of processed meteorites.

sections.title: The asteroid belt

img.alt: Animation seen from above: the Sun, the orbits of Earth and Mars, a ring of asteroids between Mars and Jupiter turning around the Sun, and two clumps of Trojan asteroids riding 60 degrees ahead of and behind Jupiter on its 12-year orbit. A few asteroids cross the inner solar system.

steps.title: Where the asteroids are
bullets: The vast majority of asteroids orbit in the **asteroid belt** between **Mars and Jupiter**.
They orbit in the **same direction** as the planets, but their orbits are generally **more elliptical** and **more tilted** to the ecliptic (up to **20-30°**).

The only other big groups are the two sets of **Trojan asteroids**, which share **Jupiter's 12-year orbit**, one group **60° ahead** of Jupiter and the other **60° behind**. NASA's **Lucy** spacecraft (launched 2021) will visit a main-belt asteroid in 2025, then seven Trojans between 2027 and 2033.
A relatively small number of asteroids have orbits through the **inner** solar system: impacts waiting to happen.

img.alt: Two tiny 1 km asteroids drawn far apart with an arrow labelled millions of kilometres between them. Note: movie asteroid fields are drama; collisions are rare and spacecraft must be steered carefully just to get close.

steps.title: Plenty of room
bullets: Science fiction shows the belt as a crowded, dangerous rock field. In reality it is so huge that typical **kilometre-size** asteroids are **millions of kilometres apart** on average.
Collisions between asteroids are **quite rare**, and spacecraft must be carefully guided just to pass close enough for a decent photo.

boxes.text: Hundreds of thousands of asteroids sound like a lot, but they are spread over a ring of space hundreds of millions of kilometres around.
Trojans: 'sixty ahead, sixty behind' Jupiter, same 12-year lap.

The asteroid belt is mostly empty space: a spacecraft crossing it is very unlikely to hit anything (Book 12.2, Common Misconceptions, p. 360). Asteroid orbits are more tilted and elliptical than the planets', but they still go the SAME direction.

sections.title: Jupiter's resonances and the Kirkwood gaps

img.alt: Animation over 12 years: Jupiter goes around the Sun once while an asteroid on a 6-year orbit goes around twice. Each time they line up in the same place a red arrow shows Jupiter's tug. The repeated nudges push the asteroid out of that orbit; the same happens for 4-year and 3-year orbits.

steps.title: What an orbital resonance is
bullets: An **orbital resonance** happens when two objects **line up periodically**. In the belt, it happens when an asteroid's orbital period is a **simple fraction** of Jupiter's, such as **1/2, 1/4 or 2/5**.
Example: an asteroid with a **6-year** period (half of Jupiter's **12** years) gets the **same gravitational nudge** from Jupiter every 12 years, so it is soon **pushed out** of that orbit.
The same happens for periods of **4 years** (1/3 of Jupiter's) and **3 years** (1/4).

img.alt: A singer's sound waves reach an open piano. The string with the same note vibrates, and so do strings whose notes have half or a quarter of its frequency. Likewise, Jupiter's repeated tugs 'ring' asteroids whose periods are simple fractions of its own.

steps.title: The piano analogy
bullets: Sing into an open piano and the strings 'in resonance' with your voice start to **vibrate**: not only the note you sing but also notes with **half or a quarter** of its frequency.
In the same way, Jupiter's repeated, well-timed tugs build up on asteroids whose periods fit neatly into its own.

img.alt: Simplified graph of the number of asteroids against orbital period, 2.5 to 7 years, with distance in AU along the top. Deep gaps appear at 3 years (1/4 of Jupiter's period), 4 years (1/3), 4.8 years (2/5) and 6 years (1/2). A separate bar at 12 years, the 1/1 resonance, shows the Trojans.

steps.title: Kirkwood gaps
bullets: A graph of how many asteroids have each orbital period shows clear **gaps** at periods in resonance with Jupiter: those orbits have been **cleared**. They are called **Kirkwood gaps**, after their discoverer.
Not every resonance makes a gap; some **gather** asteroids. The **1/1** resonance (the same period as Jupiter) is where the **Trojans** live.
The gaps show up clearly on a graph of period (or average distance), but are hard to see on a snapshot of where asteroids are, because the graph sorts asteroids by their **average** orbital distance.

boxes.text: One random tug averages out, but a tug that always comes at the same point in the orbit adds up time after time, like pushing a swing at the right moment.
Gap periods: 12 years divided by 2, 3 and 4 = 6, 4 and 3 years. Trojans: 12 / 1 = 12.

Resonance gaps are in orbital PERIOD (average distance), not empty bands in a picture of the belt on one night (Book 12.2, 'Think about it', p. 361). The 1/1 resonance collects asteroids (the Trojans) rather than clearing them.

sections.title: Why no planet formed there

img.alt: Four numbered steps: 1, the region once held enough rock for another planet; 2, repeated tugs from young Jupiter stirred up orbits; 3, planetesimals smashed together or were kicked out, later hitting a planet or moon, the Sun, or leaving the solar system; 4, the belt lost most of its mass and keeps grinding down.

steps.title: Jupiter spoiled a planet
bullets: Almost all the planetesimals that formed **inside Mars's orbit** ended up in the inner planets. Those between **Mars and Jupiter** were strongly affected by **resonances with Jupiter**, and only a small fraction kept orbits that let them stay.

Early on the region probably held **more than enough** rock to build another terrestrial planet. But the young Jupiter's resonances disrupted the planetesimals' orbits, sometimes making them **crash into each other** and sometimes **kicking them out**.
Once kicked out, they eventually **hit a planet or moon**, or were flung **out of the solar system** or **into the Sun**.

img.alt: A large circle labelled the Moon beside a smaller ball labelled all asteroids: squeezed together they would make a body under 2000 km across, just over half the Moon's diameter.

steps.title: Not much left, and still grinding
bullets: Over 4½ billion years these disruptions removed **most of the belt's original mass**. If all asteroids were squeezed into one ball, it would be **less than 2000 km** across, just over **half the Moon's diameter**: less mass than the Moon.
The belt is still changing slowly. Jupiter keeps nudging orbits, so a **major collision** happens somewhere in the belt about every **100,000 years**.

Each collision breaks large asteroids into smaller ones and makes lots of **dust**. The belt has been grinding itself down for over 4 billion years and will continue as long as the solar system exists.

boxes.text: Jupiter's resonances kept stirring the planetesimals, so instead of building up into one planet they smashed into each other or were thrown out of the region.
No planet because of Jupiter's tugs: 'Jupiter juggled the would-be planet apart.'

The asteroid belt is NOT the remains of a planet that exploded; a planet never formed there because of Jupiter (Book 12.2, p. 361). The total mass of all asteroids is less than the Moon's, despite their huge numbers.

sections.title: Why comets grow tails

img.alt: A lumpy icy nucleus speckled with dark dust, labelled ice plus rocky dust plus complex chemicals. Three cards: water and other hydrogen compounds, always seen in comet spectra; carbon dioxide and carbon monoxide, which condense only in the coldest, most distant parts of the solar nebula; complex carbon molecules that may have helped bring Earth the raw material for life.

steps.title: Dirty snowballs
bullets: Far from the Sun, small comets probably look much like small asteroids, with odd shapes because their gravity is too weak to make them round.
Their **spectra** show what we expect for bodies born in the cold outer solar system: **ice** mixed with **rocky dust** and some more complex chemicals. Hence the nickname **'dirty snowballs'**.

Spectra always show **hydrogen compounds**, including **water**, and also **carbon dioxide** and **carbon monoxide**, which condensed only in the coldest, most distant parts of the solar nebula. That confirms comets' distant origin.
Comets also contain many **complex molecules**, including carbon compounds, so they may have helped seed Earth with the **organic material** that made life possible.

img.alt: A comet near the Sun: a small nucleus inside a round coma of gas and dust; a straight blue plasma tail pointing straight away from the Sun, pushed by the solar wind; a wider, curved yellow dust tail pushed by sunlight. Nucleus 20 km or less, coma up to hundreds of thousands of km, tails up to hundreds of millions of km.

steps.title: Nucleus and coma
bullets: Far from the Sun the comet is completely **frozen**. For a comet falling sunward we call this frozen centre the **nucleus**.

As it speeds toward the Sun its surface warms and ices **vaporize** into gas, which easily escapes the comet's weak gravity. Some of the gas drags **dust** away too, making a huge, dusty atmosphere called the **coma**.

Most nuclei we have seen are **no more than about 20 km** across, yet the coma can reach **tens to hundreds of thousands of kilometres** in radius (as big as Jupiter or bigger), and tails can be **hundreds of millions of kilometres** long.

img.alt: Two comets moving away from the Sun. The crossed-out one has its tail trailing behind like a rocket's exhaust: wrong. The correct one has its tail pointing away from the Sun, which here is ahead of the comet.

steps.title: Two tails, both pointing away from the Sun
bullets: Tails do **not** trail behind the comet like rocket exhaust. They point generally **away from the Sun**, whichever way the comet is moving.
The **plasma tail** is gas **ionized** by the Sun's ultraviolet light and pushed out by the **solar wind**, so it points almost **straight away** from the Sun.
The **dust tail** is dust pushed by the much weaker pressure of **sunlight** itself (**radiation pressure**). It also points away from the Sun but **curves back** toward where the comet came from.

img.alt: Animation: a comet travels a long elliptical orbit around the Sun. Far out it is a bare frozen nucleus; inside about 5 AU a coma appears; by about 1 AU two tails grow, always pointing away from the Sun, even as the comet heads back out; between 3 and 5 AU on the way out they fade. The last frame shows the comet at several points.

steps.title: A trip around the Sun
bullets: A gas **coma** begins to form when the comet is about **5 AU** from the Sun, and the **tails** form by about **1 AU**.
After the comet loops around the Sun and heads out, vaporization declines and the coma and tails **disappear** (somewhere between 3 and 5 AU).
Then nothing happens until the comet comes sunward again: in a century, a millennium, a million years, or never.

steps.title: A short active life
bullets: Comets that keep coming back, like Halley's, cannot last long. A comet loses about **0.1% of its ice** per pass, so it can make no more than **a few hundred** passes before most of its ice is gone.
On a close pass it may shed a layer a **metre thick**. Dust too heavy to escape piles up as a **dark crust**, which may eventually stop gas escaping, so no more coma or tails.
Fates: a dust-covered dead comet may look like an **asteroid**; or it may come 'unglued' and **break apart**, or even **disintegrate** along its orbit.

boxes.text: The Sun's heat turns ice to gas, and then two different pushes act on what escapes: the solar wind on charged gas, and sunlight's gentle pressure on dust.
Plasma tail = straight, solar Wind. Dust tail = curved, sunlight. Both point AWAY from the Sun.

A comet leaving the Sun travels TAIL FIRST: tails point away from the Sun, not behind the comet (Book 12.3, p. 362). The plasma tail is pushed by the solar wind; the dust tail by sunlight (radiation pressure), not the other way round. The nucleus is small (20 km or less); it is the coma and tails that are huge.

sections.title: Visiting comets

img.alt: Timeline of comet missions: 1986, Giotto at Halley, a very dark nucleus less dense than water, with violent jets; 2004, Stardust at Wild 2, collected comet dust in aerogel; 2005, Deep Impact at Tempel 1, a 370 kg impactor revealed organic molecules and deep dust; 2014-16, Rosetta at Comet C-G, with the Philae lander.

steps.title: Giotto, Stardust and Deep Impact
bullets: **Giotto** (European Space Agency) flew past **Halley's Comet** in **1986**: the first clear view of a nucleus. It was surprisingly **dark** (reflecting under **5%** of light), **less dense than water** (so part ice, part empty space), and shot **jets** of gas and dust out at hundreds of metres per second.

**Stardust** (NASA, **2004**) caught dust from Comet **Wild 2** in **aerogel** and sent it to Earth: our first direct comet dust sample. Some of it must have formed in the **inner** solar system, then mixed with outer-solar-system material.

**Deep Impact** (NASA, July 4, **2005**) slammed a **370 kg** impactor into Comet **Tempel 1** at **37,000 km/h**. The plume held many **complex organic molecules** and so much dust that the surface must be covered by dust **tens of metres** deep.

img.alt: Cross-section of a comet surface: a dark, dusty crust of rock and carbon-bearing molecules on top, with ice below. Where the crust has collapsed into a pit, a jet of water vapour streams out into space.

steps.title: Rosetta and Philae
bullets: **Rosetta** (European Space Agency) orbited **Comet 67P/Churyumov-Gerasimenko** (Comet C-G) for about two years, **2014-2016**, from when it was nearly frozen through **perihelion** (its closest point to the Sun), watching its coma and tails grow.

Its lander **Philae** was meant to fire harpoons to anchor itself, but it **bounced twice** and tumbled into a shadowed crevice, where its batteries could not recharge. It still made the **first soft landing on a comet**, and briefly woke up when sunlight returned. At the end Rosetta itself was landed on the comet.

Rosetta found that the ice driving the comet's activity is hidden under a thick **dusty crust** of rock and carbon-bearing molecules; almost no ice is exposed. Jets of water vapour shoot from pits where the crust has **collapsed**.

img.alt: Bars comparing the ratio of heavy hydrogen (deuterium) to ordinary hydrogen in water: Earth's oceans and water-bearing primitive meteorites are about the same, while Comet C-G and several other comets are much higher. So Earth's water probably came mostly from outer-belt asteroids, though too few comets are measured to be sure.

steps.title: Did comets bring Earth's water?
bullets: Rosetta measured the ratio of **deuterium** (heavy hydrogen) to ordinary hydrogen in Comet C-G's water: **much higher** than in Earth's water. Several other comets are similar.
So comets were probably **not the main source** of the water that impacts delivered to the early Earth.

Water-bearing **primitive meteorites** have a ratio closer to Earth's, suggesting Earth's water came from asteroids formed in the **outer asteroid belt**. The debate continues, since too few comets have been measured to rule them out.

boxes.text: Water carries a chemical 'fingerprint' in its share of heavy hydrogen. Matching fingerprints point to the source; comets' fingerprint does not match Earth's oceans well.
Missions in order: G-S-D-R (Giotto 1986, Stardust 2004, Deep Impact 2005, Rosetta 2014-16).

Comet nuclei are DARK, not bright white snowballs: Halley's reflects under 5% of light (Book 12.3, p. 363). Rosetta's deuterium result argues AGAINST comets as Earth's main water source. Stardust collected dust; it did not land.

sections.title: Comet dust and meteor showers

img.alt: Top view: the Sun, Earth's round orbit and a comet's long orbit lined with a trail of sand- to pebble-size debris. Earth crosses the trail on the same date each year, giving a meteor shower. Particles hit the air at up to 250,000 km/h (70 km/s).

steps.title: The invisible third tail
bullets: Comets also shed **sand- to pebble-size** particles, too big to be pushed by the solar wind or sunlight. They form a third, **invisible tail** that follows the comet around its **orbit**.

These particles cause **most meteors** and meteor showers. They are far too small to see, but they hit the atmosphere at up to about **250,000 km/h (70 km/s)**, heating the air until it **glows**: the brief flash of a meteor.
About **25 million** comet dust particles burn up as meteors every day, adding **hundreds of tons** of comet dust to Earth daily.

img.alt: A year strip from January to December marking major annual meteor showers and their parent comets: Quadrantids January 3; Lyrids April 22, Thatcher; Eta Aquarids May 5, Halley; Perseids August 12, Swift-Tuttle; Orionids October 22, Halley; Leonids November 17, Tempel-Tuttle; Geminids December 14, Phaethon; and others.

steps.title: Meteor showers return every year
bullets: On any clear night you can usually see a **few** meteors. On nights when Earth crosses a **comet's orbit**, you may see **dozens per hour**: a **meteor shower**.

Showers **recur at about the same date each year**, because Earth passes through a particular comet's orbit at the same time each year. Examples: the **Perseids** (August 12, Comet Swift-Tuttle) and the **Orionids** (October 22, Halley's Comet).
Other planets must have showers too. After Comet Siding Spring passed close to **Mars** in 2014, the **MAVEN** spacecraft detected comet dust in Mars's upper atmosphere.

img.alt: Animation of a night sky: meteor streaks appear one after another, all pointing back to a single spot called the radiant, the way snow seems to rush out of one point in front of a moving car. In a real shower you might see one every few minutes, not all at once.

steps.title: The radiant
bullets: The meteors of a shower seem to **radiate from one point** in the sky, called the **radiant**, for the same reason snow or heavy rain seems to come from one point in front of a **moving car**: we are moving through the stream of particles.
Even in the best showers you would see one meteor only every **few minutes**; a photo that shows many at once is a composite.

img.alt: Earth drawn with a day side facing the Sun and a night side, and an arrow showing Earth's motion around the Sun. The pre-dawn part of the night side faces forward, so more particles hit it, as more snow hits a car's windshield than its rear window.

steps.title: Watch before dawn
bullets: More meteors hit Earth from the **front** than from behind, just as more snow hits a car's **windshield** than its back window.
So showers are best seen in the **pre-dawn** hours, when your part of the sky faces the **direction of Earth's motion**.

boxes.text: The particles are spread along the comet's orbit like a dusty racetrack. Earth's orbit crosses that track at the same point every year.
Perseids = August 12 (summer), Swift-Tuttle. Halley gives TWO showers: Eta Aquarids (May) and Orionids (October).
Shower meteors come mainly from the 'third tail' of sand- to pebble-size grains, NOT from the visible dust or plasma tails (Book 12.3, p. 364). The best time is before dawn, not right after sunset.

sections.title: Two reservoirs of comets

img.alt: Not to scale: a flat donut of comets just beyond the planets, the Kuiper belt, from about 30 to 50 AU with about 100,000 comets over 100 km orbiting in the planets' plane and direction; surrounded by a huge sphere of comets, the Oort cloud, reaching about 50,000 AU with about a trillion comets on randomly tilted orbits.

steps.title: How we know they are out there
bullets: We have never actually seen small comets that far from the Sun. But the comets we do see must come from **somewhere**, and **tracing their orbits back** shows where.
Counting how many new comets enter the inner solar system each year tells us how many must be waiting out there. Such studies reveal **two distinct reservoirs**.

Example of the reasoning: if about 100 new comets arrived every year for the solar system's whole history (about 4.5 billion years), at least 100 x 4.5 billion = **450 billion** comets must be in the reservoir.

img.alt: Two panels. Kuiper belt comets: orbits drawn nearly flat, in the planets' plane and all going the same way, reaching no more than about twice Neptune's distance. Oort cloud comets: long orbits tilted every which way, some going backward, coming from very far away.

steps.title: The Oort cloud
bullets: **Most** comets that visit the inner solar system do **not** orbit in the planets' direction, and their elongated orbits have **random orientations**.
Traced back, they come from far beyond the planets, sometimes nearly **a quarter of the way to the nearest star**: a vast **spherical** region called the **Oort cloud**, reaching about **50,000 AU**.
The Oort cloud is **not a cloud of gas** but a collection of individual comets, about **a trillion (10^12)** of them.

img.alt: Side-by-side comparison. Asteroid: rock and metal, formed mostly inside the frost line, mostly in the belt at 2-3 AU, no tail. Comet: ice with rocky dust, formed in the cold outer solar system, mostly in the Kuiper belt or Oort cloud, grows a coma and tails only near the Sun.

steps.title: The Kuiper belt
bullets: A **smaller** number of visiting comets follow a pattern: they orbit in the **same direction** and nearly the **same plane** as the planets, and go no more than about **twice Neptune's distance** from the Sun.
They come from the **donut-shaped Kuiper belt** beyond Neptune, about **30 to 50 AU** from the Sun, holding about **100,000 comets** more than 100 km across.

boxes.text: An orbit keeps the memory of where it came from: a comet's direction, tilt and farthest distance point back to its home reservoir.
Kuiper belt = flat donut, planets' way round, 30-50 AU. Oort cloud = giant ball, any way round, out to 50,000 AU.

The Oort cloud is a swarm of separate comets, NOT a cloud of gas (Book 12.3, p. 365). A comet on a randomly tilted or backward orbit came from the Oort cloud, not the Kuiper belt. No object in the Oort cloud has ever been seen directly.

sections.title: How the comets got there

img.alt: Animation, side view of the young solar system: icy leftovers between Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus and Neptune are flung outward in all directions by close passes and settle into a round Oort cloud, while leftovers beyond Neptune stay in the flat Kuiper belt.

steps.title: Flung out by the giant planets
bullets: Leftover icy planetesimals among **Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus and Neptune** were doomed to either **collide** with a young jovian planet or pass close to one.

When a small object passes near a large planet, the planet hardly changes but the small object can be **flung off at high speed**. Survivors were thrown in **all directions**; some escaped the solar system entirely.
The rest ended up on orbits with huge average distances: the **Oort cloud**. The **random directions** of the flings explain why it is roughly **spherical**.
Oort cloud comets are so far out that **nearby stars** (and even the galaxy's mass) can nudge them, keeping some away for good and sending others plunging toward the Sun.

img.alt: Summary cards: asteroid belt, 2-3 AU, rocky leftovers that Jupiter's gravity kept from forming a planet; Kuiper belt, 30-50 AU, icy leftovers that formed and stayed beyond Neptune, shaped by resonances; Oort cloud, out to 50,000 AU, icy leftovers flung from the jovian planet region; today, nudges still send some toward Earth.

steps.title: Left in place beyond Neptune
bullets: **Beyond Neptune**, icy planetesimals were much less likely to be thrown out. They stayed on orbits in the **planets' direction**, near the **ecliptic plane**: the comets of the **Kuiper belt**.
**Orbital resonances** with the jovian planets can nudge Kuiper belt comets onto orbits through the inner solar system.
Surprise: **Kuiper belt comets formed farther from the Sun** than Oort cloud comets, even though the Oort cloud is now **much** more distant.

img.alt: Diagram of 'Oumuamua's path: an open curve that swings in fast past the Sun, inside Mercury's orbit, and leaves forever. Notes: too fast to be bound to the Sun and never passed near Jupiter, so it formed around another star; about 250 m long, no gas or dust; a second visitor, 2I/Borisov, was found in 2019.

steps.title: A visitor from another star
bullets: Until 2017, every object seen in our solar system had an orbit consistent with having always belonged to it. Then the **Pan-STARRS** telescopes in Hawai'i found **'Oumuamua** ('scout'), moving so fast it had **escape velocity** from the solar system.

Traced back, it had entered at high speed without passing near Jupiter or anything else that could have changed its orbit: the first confirmed object from **around another star**. It is small (perhaps **250 m** long) and released no detectable gas or dust, so it is more like an **asteroid** than a comet.

This was not totally unexpected: our own solar system has probably **ejected** vast numbers of asteroids and comets, so others must have too. A second visitor, **2I/Borisov**, was found in **2019**, and the new **Vera C. Rubin Observatory** should find many more.

boxes.text: Close passes by giant planets act like gravitational slingshots: they hurl small bodies outward in random directions, building a round cloud from material that started in a flat disk.
Oort comets = 'kicked out' (from the jovian zone). Kuiper comets = 'stayed put' (beyond Neptune).

Oort cloud comets did NOT form where they are now: they formed among the jovian planets and were flung out, so they formed CLOSER to the Sun than Kuiper belt comets (Book 12.3, p. 366). 'Oumuamua behaved like an asteroid, not a comet: it released no gas or dust.

quiz.q: What is the main difference between an asteroid and a comet?
options: Asteroids orbit the Sun while comets orbit planets
Asteroids are rocky while comets are ice-rich
Comets are always larger than asteroids
Asteroids have tails while comets do not
Comets orbit in the opposite direction to asteroids
quiz.why: Both orbit the Sun and are too small to be planets; the basic difference is composition: asteroids are rocky leftover planetesimals, comets icy ones. Most comets never grow tails, and asteroids never do.
