quiz.why: Eris is about the same size as Pluto but about 27% more massive. If Pluto was a planet, Eris should be one too, and then what about slightly smaller objects? The IAU created the dwarf planet category in 2006.

img.alt: Pluto and Eris drawn side by side at about the same size. Eris, found in 2005, is about 27% more massive than Pluto and has a moon, Dysnomia. Question below: if Pluto is a planet, must Eris be one too, and what about slightly smaller bodies?

quiz.q: A friend says, 'I picked up a meteor in the field after last night's fireball.' What is wrong with this?
options: A meteor is the flash of light; the rock is a meteorite
Nothing: a meteor is a rock found on the ground
Fireballs never leave rocks on the ground
A meteor is a comet's tail, not a rock
Meteorites only ever land in the ocean
quiz.why: A meteor is only the flash of light made as a particle enters the atmosphere. A rock that survives and reaches the ground is a meteorite. Fireballs are exactly the bright meteors that can leave meteorites.

img.alt: Three cards. Meteor, meaning a thing in the air: the flash of light when dust or rock hits the air at high speed. Fireball: an unusually bright meteor made by a rock big enough to survive. Meteorite, meaning associated with meteors: the rock found on the ground.

quiz.q: Why do most meteors never produce a meteorite?
options: They are pulled back into space by Earth's magnetic field
Most of the particles are pea-size or smaller and burn up completely
They are made of ice, which melts in the air
They mostly fall at night when no one sees them
Earth's gravity is too weak to pull them down
quiz.why: The vast majority of meteor particles are no larger than peas and burn up completely before reaching the ground. Only rare, larger rocks survive.

img.alt: Animation of the sky above the ground. A pea-size grain streaks in and burns up completely high in the air: a meteor. A larger rock makes a very bright fireball all the way down and lands as a dark stone: a meteorite.

quiz.q: Which observation is the strongest evidence that most meteorites come from the asteroid belt?
options: Paths of observed falls trace back to the asteroid belt
Some meteorites attract a magnet
Meteorites have a dark, pitted crust
Most meteorites land in the ocean
Meteorites contain iridium
quiz.why: The most direct evidence is the meteorites whose falls were observed or filmed: in every case their trajectories traced back to the asteroid belt. The crust, metal and iridium show a rock is from space, not where in space.

img.alt: Map of the inner solar system: a big arrow brings meteorites from the asteroid belt to Earth; a thin dashed arrow brings a few from Mars, and a few come from the Moon. Almost all meteorites are tiny asteroids or pieces of them; lunar and martian meteorites were blasted off by impacts.

quiz.q: Which of these would NOT help show that a rock is a meteorite?
options: A dark, pitted crust
Enough metal to attract a magnet
Unusually high iridium
A smooth, rounded shape like a river pebble
Isotope ratios unlike Earth rocks
quiz.why: Clues are a dark, pitted crust from the fiery fall, high metal content, elements such as iridium that are rare on Earth, and unusual isotope ratios. A water-smoothed shape is typical of ordinary Earth rocks.

img.alt: Four clue cards: 1, a dark, pitted crust from the fiery fall; 2, metal-rich enough to pull a magnet on a string; 3, rare elements such as iridium; 4, isotope ratios unlike Earth rocks. Lab analysis is the final test.

quiz.q: Two asteroids of similar size are equally bright in visible light. Infrared shows Asteroid 1 is more reflective than Asteroid 2. Which is farther away?
options: Whichever one is rotating faster
Asteroid 2
They are at the same distance
It cannot be told without a spacecraft
Asteroid 1
quiz.why: At equal size, the more reflective Asteroid 1 would look brighter at the same distance. Since both look equally bright, Asteroid 1 must be farther away.

img.alt: A large dark asteroid and a smaller shiny one look equally bright in visible light. The dark one absorbs more sunlight, so it is warmer and brighter in infrared. Comparing visible and infrared gives reflectivity; with distance from the orbit, the size follows: the darker one must be bigger.

quiz.q: An asteroid's brightness rises and falls twice in each rotation even though its surface is evenly bright. This suggests it is:
options: Elongated, not spherical
Perfectly spherical
Made mostly of ice
Losing gas like a comet
Orbited by a small moon
quiz.why: A nonspherical asteroid reflects more light when it presents its larger side to the Sun and to us, so its brightness varies as it turns.

img.alt: Animation: a long potato-shaped asteroid spins while a graph of its brightness is drawn. The brightness rises when the long side faces us and falls when the end faces us, giving two peaks per turn.

quiz.q: Mathilde and Eros look similar, but Mathilde's density is 1.5 g/cm³ and Eros's is 2.4 g/cm³. What is the best conclusion?
options: Mathilde is mostly iron
Mathilde must be a comet
Eros must be made mostly of ice
Mathilde is a loosely bound rubble pile
Eros is much younger
quiz.why: Eros's 2.4 g/cm³ is about right for solid rock. Mathilde's 1.5 g/cm³ is so low that it must be a loose rubble pile with gaps, held by weak gravity.

img.alt: Bar chart of density: Eros 2.4 grams per cubic centimetre, close to solid rock; Mathilde 1.5, a loose rubble pile; water 1.0 for comparison; Halley's comet nucleus below 1, ice plus empty space.

quiz.q: Asteroid A has the same mass as Asteroid B but twice the volume. Compared with B, A's density is:
options: Twice as large
The same
Half as large
Four times as large
A quarter as large
quiz.why: Density = mass / volume. Same mass divided by twice the volume gives half the density.

quiz.q: How do astronomers measure the mass of the asteroid Ida?
options: From its brightness and colour
By timing its rotation
From its spectrum
From the period and distance of its moon Dactyl
From radar echoes
quiz.why: Mass is measured from gravity's effect on another object. Dactyl's orbital period and distance, used in Newton's version of Kepler's third law, give Ida's mass.

img.alt: Animation: the tiny moon Dactyl circles the elongated asteroid Ida. Measuring the moon's orbital period and distance, then using Newton's version of Kepler's third law, gives Ida's mass.

quiz.q: What best explains why Vesta is much wider than it is tall?
options: It spins so fast that it flattened
Jupiter's tides stretched it
It formed from two asteroids that stuck together
Ice at its poles vaporized away
A huge impact gouged out a crater at its south pole
quiz.why: Vesta is nearly 25% wider than tall, probably because an impact dug a giant south-polar crater; it was likely once much rounder. Fast spin explains Haumea's shape, not Vesta's.

img.alt: Cut-away of Vesta: a flattened ball, nearly 25% wider than tall, with a metal core, a rocky mantle and a crust, and a huge south-pole crater with a 23 km high central peak. Notes: rock at the crater floor matches deep interior rock and many meteorites; signs of volcanic rock but no volcanoes seen; ridges ring the equator.

quiz.q: Primitive meteorites are dated at 4.56 billion years. What does this age tell us?
options: When Earth's oceans formed
When the first comets struck Earth
When Jupiter finished forming
When the asteroid belt lost most of its mass
When accretion in the solar nebula began
quiz.why: Primitive meteorites are unchanged since they accreted in the solar nebula and are the oldest rocks known, so 4.56 billion years marks when accretion began.

img.alt: Timeline from 4.56 billion years ago to today: primitive meteorites date from 4.56 billion years ago, when the first solids began to clump together; processed meteorites date from a few million years later, after some asteroids melted; today vast numbers of leftovers still orbit the Sun.

quiz.q: A newly found meteorite is rocky, full of carbon compounds and contains a little water. Where did it most likely form?
options: Inside Mercury's orbit
In the inner asteroid belt, near Mars
On the surface of the Moon
In the outer asteroid belt, beyond about 2.5 AU
In the core of a shattered asteroid
quiz.why: Carbon compounds could condense only beyond about 2.5 AU, and water near the frost line (perhaps 2.7 AU). Carbon-rich meteorites match the dark asteroids of the outer belt.

img.alt: Distance scale from the Sun out to 4 AU. Inside 2.5 AU only metal and rock condensed: stony primitive meteorites from the inner belt. Beyond 2.5 AU carbon compounds could condense, and the frost line may have been as close as 2.7 AU: carbon-rich primitive meteorites, some with water, from the outer belt.

quiz.q: Metal-rich processed meteorites are best explained as:
options: Pieces of the cores of differentiated asteroids that were shattered
Metal flakes that condensed first from the nebula
Rocks blasted off Mars
Frozen comet dust
Lava from the surface of Vesta
quiz.why: They are dense iron and nickel, like planetary cores: fragments of large asteroids that differentiated and were later broken apart in collisions.

img.alt: Animation: a rocky asteroid heats up and melts inside; metal dots sink to the centre and rock rises, making a core, mantle and crust. Then a collision shatters it. Core pieces become metal-rich processed meteorites; mantle and crust pieces become rocky processed meteorites.

quiz.q: Which statement about rocky processed meteorites is NOT correct?
options: They come from the mantles or crusts of differentiated worlds
Some are very close to volcanic basalts
They are older than primitive meteorites
Some seem to come from Vesta
They date to only millions of years after the solar system formed
quiz.why: Processed meteorites are slightly YOUNGER than primitive ones. The other statements are all true.

quiz.q: Rocky processed meteorites that formed in lava flows date to only millions of years after the solar system's birth. What does that imply?
options: Their parent asteroids are still volcanically active
They formed before the Sun did
Volcanic activity on those asteroids was short-lived
They came from Earth
All asteroids were once volcanic
quiz.why: Since the volcanic rocks are only millions of years younger than the solar system, the active period was brief: the interiors of those asteroids must have cooled quickly.

img.alt: Three cards from small to large: small asteroids are geologically dead with only craters; bodies a few hundred kilometres and up had enough heat to melt and differentiate; Vesta and a few dozen others were volcanically active early on, but only briefly before cooling.

quiz.q: An asteroid has an orbital period of exactly 4 years. What would you predict?
options: It will be captured as a moon of Mars
Nothing: Jupiter is too far away to matter
It will gather other asteroids into a Trojan group
It will slowly spiral into the Sun
Repeated tugs from Jupiter will push it out of that orbit
quiz.why: 4 years is 1/3 of Jupiter's 12-year period, an orbital resonance. Jupiter's nudges come again and again at the same points, so the orbit gets cleared (a Kirkwood gap).

img.alt: Animation over 12 years: Jupiter goes around the Sun once while an asteroid on a 6-year orbit goes around twice. Each time they line up in the same place a red arrow shows Jupiter's tug. The repeated nudges push the asteroid out of that orbit; the same happens for 4-year and 3-year orbits.

quiz.q: Not every resonance with Jupiter clears out asteroids. The 1/1 resonance (same period as Jupiter) instead holds:
options: The Trojan asteroids
The Kirkwood gaps
The Kuiper belt
The near-Earth asteroids
Ceres and Vesta
quiz.why: The Trojan asteroids share Jupiter's 12-year orbit, 60° ahead and 60° behind it: the 1/1 resonance gathers asteroids rather than clearing them.

img.alt: Simplified graph of the number of asteroids against orbital period, 2.5 to 7 years, with distance in AU along the top. Deep gaps appear at 3 years (1/4 of Jupiter's period), 4 years (1/3), 4.8 years (2/5) and 6 years (1/2). A separate bar at 12 years, the 1/1 resonance, shows the Trojans.

quiz.q: Why did no full-size planet form between Mars and Jupiter?
options: There was never enough rock in that region
The Sun's heat vaporized the planetesimals there
Orbital resonances with young Jupiter disrupted the planetesimals
A planet formed there but later exploded
The region was too cold for rock to condense
quiz.why: The region probably held enough rock for another terrestrial planet, but Jupiter's resonances stirred up the planetesimals, making them smash together or get kicked out, so most of the mass was lost.

img.alt: Four numbered steps: 1, the region once held enough rock for another planet; 2, repeated tugs from young Jupiter stirred up orbits; 3, planetesimals smashed together or were kicked out, later hitting a planet or moon, the Sun, or leaving the solar system; 4, the belt lost most of its mass and keeps grinding down.

quiz.q: If all the asteroids were gathered and squeezed into one ball, about how big would it be?
options: Larger than Earth
About the size of Mars
About 10 km across
Under 2000 km across, about half the Moon's size
About the size of Jupiter
quiz.why: Despite their huge numbers, asteroids add up to little mass: combined into a sphere they would be under 2000 km across, just over half the Moon's diameter.

img.alt: A large circle labelled the Moon beside a smaller ball labelled all asteroids: squeezed together they would make a body under 2000 km across, just over half the Moon's diameter.

quiz.q: A comet has passed the Sun and is now heading back out to the outer solar system. Which way do its tails point?
options: Behind the comet, back toward the Sun
Away from the Sun, roughly ahead of the comet
Straight up out of the ecliptic
Toward Jupiter
It has no tails while moving outward
quiz.why: Tails point generally away from the Sun regardless of the comet's direction of travel, so an outbound comet travels tail first (until its tails fade between about 3 and 5 AU).

img.alt: Two comets moving away from the Sun. The crossed-out one has its tail trailing behind like a rocket's exhaust: wrong. The correct one has its tail pointing away from the Sun, which here is ahead of the comet.

quiz.q: A comet shows a straight bluish tail and a curved, broader tail. What pushes the straight one?
options: Sunlight's radiation pressure acting on dust
Jupiter's gravity
The solar wind acting on ionized gas
Gas jets from the nucleus
The comet's own orbital motion
quiz.why: The plasma tail is gas ionized by ultraviolet light and pushed by the solar wind almost straight away from the Sun. The curved dust tail is pushed by the weaker pressure of sunlight.

img.alt: A comet near the Sun: a small nucleus inside a round coma of gas and dust; a straight blue plasma tail pointing straight away from the Sun, pushed by the solar wind; a wider, curved yellow dust tail pushed by sunlight. Nucleus 20 km or less, coma up to hundreds of thousands of km, tails up to hundreds of millions of km.

quiz.q: Which is NOT part of how a comet forms its coma and tails?
options: The nucleus melts into liquid water that streams behind it
Ices vaporize into gas that escapes its weak gravity
Escaping gas drags dust off the nucleus
Its surface warms as it nears the Sun
Gas and dust are pushed away from the Sun
quiz.why: Comet ices vaporize directly into gas; there is no liquid stream. The gas drags dust to make the coma, and gas and dust are pushed away from the Sun to form tails.

img.alt: Animation: a comet travels a long elliptical orbit around the Sun. Far out it is a bare frozen nucleus; inside about 5 AU a coma appears; by about 1 AU two tails grow, always pointing away from the Sun, even as the comet heads back out; between 3 and 5 AU on the way out they fade. The last frame shows the comet at several points.

quiz.q: Rosetta found that water in Comet C-G has a much higher ratio of deuterium to ordinary hydrogen than Earth's water. What does this suggest?
options: Asteroids contain no water at all
All of Earth's water came from comets
Earth's water came from the Sun
Comet C-G formed inside Earth's orbit
Comets were probably not the main source of Earth's water
quiz.why: The mismatch suggests comets were not the primary source. Water-bearing primitive meteorites have a ratio closer to Earth's, pointing to outer-belt asteroids, though too few comets have been measured to rule them out entirely.

img.alt: Bars comparing the ratio of heavy hydrogen (deuterium) to ordinary hydrogen in water: Earth's oceans and water-bearing primitive meteorites are about the same, while Comet C-G and several other comets are much higher. So Earth's water probably came mostly from outer-belt asteroids, though too few comets are measured to be sure.

quiz.q: Why do meteor showers happen at about the same date every year?
options: Comets return to the inner solar system every year
Earth passes through a particular comet's orbit and debris at the same time each year
The Moon's phases trigger them
Jupiter's orbit lines up with Earth once a year
Solar flares peak each year at that time
quiz.why: Comets shed sand- to pebble-size particles along their orbits. Earth crosses a given comet's orbit at the same point in its own orbit, so on the same date, each year.

img.alt: Top view: the Sun, Earth's round orbit and a comet's long orbit lined with a trail of sand- to pebble-size debris. Earth crosses the trail on the same date each year, giving a meteor shower. Particles hit the air at up to 250,000 km/h (70 km/s).

quiz.q: You see a comet arrive on an orbit tilted steeply to the planets' orbits and going around the Sun backward. It most likely came from:
options: The asteroid belt
The Oort cloud
The Kuiper belt
Jupiter's Trojan points
The surface of Mars
quiz.why: Kuiper belt comets orbit in the planets' plane and direction. Comets with random tilts and directions come from the spherical Oort cloud.

img.alt: Two panels. Kuiper belt comets: orbits drawn nearly flat, in the planets' plane and all going the same way, reaching no more than about twice Neptune's distance. Oort cloud comets: long orbits tilted every which way, some going backward, coming from very far away.

quiz.q: Where did the comets of the Oort cloud originally form?
options: In the Oort cloud itself, far from the Sun
Around other stars
In the asteroid belt
Among the jovian planets, then flung outward
Inside Mercury's orbit
quiz.why: Icy planetesimals between the jovian planets were flung out in all directions by close encounters; those that did not escape became the Oort cloud. So Kuiper belt comets actually formed farther from the Sun than Oort cloud comets.

img.alt: Animation, side view of the young solar system: icy leftovers between Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus and Neptune are flung outward in all directions by close passes and settle into a round Oort cloud, while leftovers beyond Neptune stay in the flat Kuiper belt.

quiz.q: Suppose 100 comets entered the inner solar system for the first time every year for 4.5 billion years. What is the minimum number that must have been waiting in a distant reservoir?
options: About 4,500
About 450 billion
About 450 million
About 100
About 4.5 billion
quiz.why: Each comet makes its first visit only once, so the reservoir must hold at least 100 per year x 4.5 billion years = 4.5 x 10^11, about 450 billion. (The Oort cloud is estimated at about a trillion.)

quiz.q: How can you identify an asteroid in a long exposure taken of stars through a telescope? (Assume the telescope is tracking the sky with Earth's rotation, so that stars appear as points of light.)
options: The asteroid will appear as a streak because of its motion relative to the stars.
The asteroid will be recognizable by its long, fuzzy tail.
The asteroid will be much dimmer than the surrounding stars.
The asteroid will have a noticeable circular disk, rather than being just a point of light like the stars.
The asteroid will be much brighter than the surrounding stars.
quiz.why: An asteroid moves against the background stars during the exposure, so it leaves a short streak while the tracked stars stay points. Asteroids have no tails and are too small to show disks.

quiz.q: According to the nebular theory, what are the comets and asteroids?
options: leftover planetesimals that never accreted into planets
the shattered remains of collisions between moons
the shattered remains of collisions between planets
chunks of rock or ice that condensed long after the planets had formed
chunks of rock or ice that have been expelled from the planets by volcanoes
quiz.why: Asteroids (rocky) and comets (icy) are leftover planetesimals from the solar nebula that never became part of a planet.

quiz.q: Can an asteroid also be a dwarf planet?
options: No; asteroids are too big to be considered "dwarfs."
No; dwarf planets have different compositions from asteroids.
Yes, if the asteroid is large enough for its gravity to have made it round.
Yes, all asteroids are considered to be dwarf planets.
quiz.why: A dwarf planet is round from its own gravity but has not cleared its orbit. Ceres, the largest asteroid, is round, so it counts as both an asteroid and a dwarf planet.

quiz.q: When you see the bright flash of a meteor, what are you actually seeing?
options: a bright star moving quickly past our solar system
the flash that occurs when a speeding rock from space hits the ground
emission of visible light from a particle that has not yet entered Earth's atmosphere
the glow from a pea-size particle and the surrounding air as the particle burns up in our atmosphere
a star that has suddenly shot across the sky
quiz.why: A meteor is the flash of light from a small particle (often pea-size or smaller) and the air around it heating up as it enters the atmosphere at high speed.

quiz.q: Why don't most of the particles that make meteors actually reach the surface of Earth?
options: They are too small and burn up in the atmosphere.
They are too small and are slowed to a stop in the atmosphere.
They are deflected by the solar wind.
They reflect off the atmosphere and return to space.
They are deflected by the gravity of the Moon.
quiz.why: Most meteor particles are tiny and vaporize completely from the heat of entry high in the atmosphere.

quiz.q: Which of the following would be the strongest clue that a rock you have found is a meteorite rather than a terrestrial rock?
options: It contains elements and isotopes in proportions that are rare on Earth but common in asteroids.
It contains a lot of iron.
It is dark colored.
It is too heavy for you to hold in your hand.
quiz.why: Plenty of Earth rocks are dark, heavy or iron-rich. The convincing test is chemistry: elements such as iridium and isotope ratios that match asteroids rather than Earth's crust.

quiz.q: How does the largest asteroid, Ceres, compare in size to other solar system worlds?
options: It is about a quarter the diameter of our Moon.
It is larger than Mercury but smaller than Mars.
It is larger than the planet Mars.
It is larger than our Moon but smaller than Mercury.
It is about the size of the two moons of Mars.
quiz.why: Ceres is about 1000 km across, while the Moon is about 3500 km, so Ceres is roughly a quarter of the Moon's diameter.

quiz.q: Why aren't small asteroids spherical in shape?
options: Small asteroids have odd shapes because they were all chipped off larger objects.
Large asteroids became spherical because many small collisions chipped off pieces until only a sphere was left; this did not occur with small asteroids.
The strength of gravity of small asteroids is less than the strength of the rock.
Small asteroids spin too fast for their material to settle into a ball.
quiz.why: Only an object's own gravity can pull it into a ball. In a small asteroid, gravity is too weak to overcome the strength of the rock, so it keeps a lumpy shape.

quiz.q: Which of the following best explains the origin of metal-rich meteorites?
options: They are fragments of rock chipped off the planet Mars.
They are fragments of rock chipped off the planet Mercury.
They are fragments of comets rather than of asteroids.
They are fragments of the core of an asteroid that was shattered by a collision.
They are leftover chunks of rock from the earliest period in the formation of the solar system.
quiz.why: Metal-rich (processed) meteorites come from large asteroids that melted and differentiated, with metal sinking to a core, and were later shattered by collisions. The leftover-from-formation option describes primitive meteorites.

quiz.q: How can meteorites from the Moon or Mars have made it to Earth?
options: Impacts on those worlds blasted rocks into space that eventually fell to Earth.
The solar wind gradually blew material off of the surfaces of these worlds, and once in space it collected together to make the meteorites.
The meteorites from the Moon and Mars were never actually part of those worlds; they are just rocks that formed in the same vicinities of the solar system.
Those worlds spin rapidly enough to have sent some rocks from their surfaces into space.
quiz.why: Large impacts on the Moon or Mars blasted surface rocks fast enough to escape. Some of those rocks later crossed Earth's orbit and landed here.

quiz.q: If all of the asteroids in the solar system were gathered into a single object, how big would it be once gravity compressed it?
options: about half the diameter of Earth's Moon
about the size of the Earth
about the size of Earth's Moon
about the size of a Neptune
quiz.why: All the asteroids together would make an object less than 2000 km across, just over half the Moon's diameter. The total mass is far less than the Moon's.

quiz.q: Where are the Trojan asteroids found?
options: on orbits that cross Mars's orbit
in the center of the asteroid belt
orbiting Jupiter
along Jupiter's orbit, 60° ahead of and behind Jupiter
on orbits that cross Earth's orbit
quiz.why: Trojan asteroids share Jupiter's orbit around the Sun, gathered at two stable points 60° ahead of and behind the planet. They orbit the Sun, not Jupiter.

quiz.q: Gaps in the asteroid belt occur at distances where
options: the period of an orbiting asteroid would be the same as Jupiter's orbital period.
the density of asteroids was once so high that collisions pulverized the asteroids into dust.
the period of an orbiting asteroid would be the same as Mars's orbital period.
the period of an orbiting asteroid would be a simple fraction (like 1/3 or 1/4) of Jupiter's orbital period.
the orbit would take the asteroid beyond the "frost line" in the solar system.
quiz.why: At orbital resonances with Jupiter (a period of 1/2, 1/3 and so on of Jupiter's 12 years), repeated tugs at the same point push asteroids out of those orbits, leaving the Kirkwood gaps.

quiz.q: According to the nebular theory, what is the asteroid belt?
options: It consists of planetesimals formed in the outer solar system that were flung into distant orbits by encounters with the jovian planets.
It consists of planetesimals that formed beyond Neptune's orbit and never accreted to form a planet.
It is material left over from the interstellar cloud that never contracted with the rest of the gases to form the solar nebula.
It consists of planetesimals that formed between the orbits of Mars and Jupiter but which Jupiter's gravity prevented from becoming a planet.
It consists of objects that fragmented from the Sun during a catastrophic collision early in the formation of the solar system.
quiz.why: Rocky planetesimals between Mars and Jupiter never built a planet because Jupiter's resonances stirred them up, so their collisions shattered rather than merged them. The 'flung outward' option describes the Oort cloud and the 'beyond Neptune' option the Kuiper belt.

quiz.q: When a comet is in the inner solar system, what part of it points most directly away from the Sun?
options: the denser side of its nucleus
its coma
jets of gas emerging from its nucleus
its tail
quiz.why: Comet tails point away from the Sun: the plasma (ion) tail is pushed straight back by the solar wind, and the dust tail curves gently behind it.

quiz.q: A comet that has an extremely elliptical orbit most likely came from
options: outside the solar system.
the Oort cloud.
the Kuiper belt.
the Trojan asteroids.
the asteroid belt.
quiz.why: Oort cloud comets fall in from very far away on long, highly elongated orbits at random tilts. Kuiper belt comets have more ordered orbits near the plane of the planets.

order.title: A comet's trip past the Sun
order.prompt: Put the stages in order, first at the bottom.
order.why: Far out the nucleus is frozen; at about 5 AU ice vaporizes and a coma forms; by about 1 AU tails form pointing away from the Sun; after rounding the Sun, the coma and tails fade between 3 and 5 AU.

layers.name: Frozen nucleus far from the Sun
Ice vaporizes; a coma forms (about 5 AU)
Tails form, pointing away from the Sun (about 1 AU)
The comet swings around the Sun
Coma and tails fade (3-5 AU outbound)

order.title: From the Sun outward
order.prompt: Order these by distance from the Sun, closest at the bottom.
order.why: Mars, then the main asteroid belt (2-3 AU), then Jupiter and its Trojans (about 5 AU), then Neptune, the Kuiper belt (30-50 AU) and finally the Oort cloud (out to about 50,000 AU).

order.title: From planetesimal to processed meteorite
order.prompt: Put the steps in order, first at the bottom.
order.why: An asteroid accretes from nebula material, heats and melts inside, differentiates (metal sinks, rock rises), is shattered by a collision, and a fragment eventually falls to Earth.

order.title: Understanding comets through history
order.prompt: Order these events in time, earliest at the bottom.
order.why: Tycho showed in 1577 that a comet was beyond the Moon; Newton showed comets orbit the Sun about a century later; Halley calculated his comet's orbit in 1705; it returned in 1758; Giotto visited it in 1986.

layers.name: Tycho: a comet lies beyond the Moon

sort.title: Asteroid or comet?

items.text: Formed mostly inside the frost line
Grows a coma near the Sun
From the Kuiper belt or Oort cloud

sort.why: Asteroids are rocky, formed inside the frost line, live mostly in the belt and supply most meteorites. Comets are icy, come from the Kuiper belt or Oort cloud, contain ices like CO and grow comas and tails near the Sun.

sort.title: Primitive or processed meteorite?

items.text: Came from a body that melted

sort.why: Primitive meteorites (chondrites) are unchanged since the nebula: the oldest rocks, stony or carbon-rich. Processed ones (achondrites) come from differentiated bodies: metal-rich cores or rocky mantles and crusts, such as Vesta's.

sort.title: Kuiper belt or Oort cloud?
sort.prompt: Sort each fact into the comet reservoir it describes.

items.text: Orbits in the planets' plane and direction
Comets flung out by jovian planets

sort.why: The Kuiper belt is a flat donut beyond Neptune where comets formed and stayed. The Oort cloud is a huge sphere of about a trillion comets flung out from the jovian region, nudged by passing stars.

sort.title: Plasma tail or dust tail?

items.text: Points straight away from the Sun
Curves back along the comet's path

sort.why: The plasma tail is ionized gas swept straight back by the solar wind. The dust tail is pushed by the weaker pressure of sunlight, so it curves slightly back toward where the comet came from.

Learning objectives are the book's learning-goal questions for 12.1-12.3. The book phrases the fourth as 'What do meteorites tell us about asteroids and the early solar system?' in the section heading.
All pictures are original diagrams (gen_*) drawn from the ideas in the reading; no book figures or photos are used. The Kirkwood-gap graph is a simplified shape, not the book's data.
The 'Oumuamua Special Topic is taught in the 'How the comets got there' section as a contrast.
